articles.title: What on Earth Is Dekton?
articles.content: This is our fifth article from Issue 26, which arrived with print subscribers last week. In it, Charles C Mann explains how he learned to love porcelain. I am aware that I am a bit of a kitchen equipment nerd, okay? So maybe you don’t have to roll your eyes theatrically like my cousins did when I tell you my wife and I got a swanky induction cooktop that was, well, kind of pricey for a middle-class couple? And maybe you can imagine my irritation when it turned out that the swanky induction cooktop – did I mention it was pricey? – did not include the necessary smooth cooking surface above the induction burners, and that you had to buy the cooking surface separately from a separate company, a fact not exactly advertised on the website, and that the surface could not be tempered glass, which is what I had thought was on top of induction ranges, a sheet of which costs maybe $30 per square foot, but a special, newly created material called Dekton that cost five times as much. ‘What on earth is Dekton?’ I asked the heavens, or at least my wife. My question turned out to have two answers. The first is that Dekton is an artificial material invented by the Spanish company Cosentino in 2013 that is amazingly heat-, pressure-, scratch-, shatter-, and stain-resistant – a high-tech substance that would have been almost impossible to fashion even thirty years ago. The other answer, equally true, is that Dekton is basically porcelain. Paradoxically, porcelain is both one of humankind’s oldest high technologies and one of its newest. The earliest proto-porcelain was created more than three thousand years ago, and was, for the time, an astonishing technical feat, as unprecedented as the roughly concurrent development of iron metallurgy. Iron technology had its second flowering in the mid-nineteenth century, when the invention of the Bessemer and Siemens-Martin refining processes allowed manufacturers to produce cheap, high-quality steel. Porcelain is having its resurgence today – indeed, high-tech ceramics are key elements in the ongoing upsurge in materials science, the study of the relationship between a substance’s structure and its physical properties. Much attention is rightfully focused now on the rise of the digital world and the explosive arrival of artificial intelligence. But that attention sometimes obscures the ongoing, equally important transformation of our physical world, the built environment, by materials science. Unleashing a cataract of innovation so ubiquitous as to be almost invisible, materials science has literally changed the walls around us. Porcelain is a reminder that the drive to create new types of matter has long played a powerful role in human history. The initial steps toward porcelain occurred when potters in northern China started to tinker with an unusual clay, chalk colored and fine grained, called kaolin. articles.title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
articles.content: “It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained. We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards. Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy. ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information where it came from. Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “ A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma ”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. This mystery led to an amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds and a bounty for anyone who could find them . The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase: “I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don’t know details. The message was along the lines of ‘Give Bob and Jerry a raise’ or ‘Bob and Jerry rule’ or something like that. It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn’t remember the details either. Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they are no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant.” Jerry Solinas, 2015 Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived. Claude found the seeds Several Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of a humorous phrase. That turned out to be wrong. In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue. In under half an hour , Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s lrand48 random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp! articles.title: FLUX 3 Image Klein
articles.content: Today we are releasing FLUX 3 Image Klein, a 5.6B parameter open weights model for text-to-image generation, image editing and multi-reference generation with up to 10 reference images. It shares core capabilities with the full FLUX 3 Image model: native 4K generation, pixel-perfect editing, and bounding boxes that control where elements are placed or confine edits to a defined area. FLUX 3 Image Klein builds on FLUX 3's shared learnings across images, video and audio. Images contribute spatial detail, video adds motion and physical dynamics, and audio provides information about events and interactions. Together, these signals help the model generate images that feel grounded in the real world. The release includes a base model for fine-tuning and a step distilled model for low-latency generation, along with FP8, INT8 and NVFP4 builds developed with NVIDIA support, under the FLUX Kommunity License. Try it in the BFL API · Download the weights Leading open weights quality with fewer parameters In internal evaluations, FLUX 3 Image Klein ranks first in text-to-image, multi-reference generation and image editing, ahead of larger open weights models. It also rates above the closed models in the comparison, Ideogram V4.5 and FLUX.2 [pro]. At 5.6B parameters, it is the smallest open model in the comparison, against 7B for Qwen-Image 2.1 and 12.9B for Krea 2. Compared with FLUX.2 [klein] 9B, it gains 91 Elo in text-to-image and 70 in image editing, with 38% fewer parameters. Parameter counts are for the image generator, as each publisher reports them; text encoders are not counted. Krea 2 does not support image editing and is not included in the image editing comparison. FLUX 3 Image Klein was also optimized for consumer GPUs. Fewer parameters make it practical to run locally and cheaper to adapt, and teams with data sovereignty or local deployment requirements can evaluate and adapt the model on their own infrastructure. This is also key for on-device image editing, allowing consumers to edit images directly on their favorite laptops. The generator weights require 11.2 GB in BF16 and 5.6 GB in FP8. With the INT8 build, FLUX 3 Image Klein runs on NVIDIA GeForce RTX GPUs with as little as 8GB of VRAM, through ComfyUI or Diffusers, extending what FLUX.2 [klein] started to even smaller hardware. With the distilled model and the INT8 build, it generates a 1MP image in about 4 seconds on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 and under 9 seconds on an RTX 4070 through ComfyUI. articles.title: You could have invented transformers from memory
articles.content: Retrieving a character from memory. The recall worsens as the number of memories grows. Large language models today can recall obscure facts from every corner of the world. Most recently, I was running late for a friend’s board game night, so I asked Astra to remind me the rules to Dune: Imperium. It gladly narrated them to me as I drove over and helped me remember the rules well enough for me to play again. We’re so used to asking models about anything that we take their vast knowledge for granted. How do models remember so much information? And how much can they store? In this post, I’ll go through an intuitive way to look at linear maps, MLPs, and self-attention as different kinds of memory stores. From this intuition we can derive some heuristics for how much memory each layer can store. The key property that characterizes a “good” memory store is its ability to recall what it stored. After all, even if we could store infinitely many facts, it’s not very helpful if we can’t recall them when we need to. The more memories we store, the more they interfere with each other when we try to recall one. So throughout the post we’ll focus on one quantity, the interference-to-signal ratio, which measures how much the other memories get in the way during recall. The number of memories a store can hold before the interference grows as large as the signal is its capacity . We’ll develop this perspective and show how you can go from a linear layer to something better, an MLP, which improves both capacity and recall, and then all the way to self-attention, which has very good recall and can store a potentially unbounded number of memories. With 64-dimensional keys, that’s a jump from about 64 memories, to about 2,700, to over a million. Here are the terms we’ll use throughout. A memory store is a function $f$ that holds $M$ memories, for $i = 1, \ldots, M$. A memory is one key-value pair: a key $k_i \in \reals^{d_k}$, used for lookup based on similarity, and a value $v_i \in \reals^{d_v}$, which is what we want to retrieve. To use $f$, we query it with an input $x$, and it recalls an output $f(x)$. A good memory store recalls $v_i$ when we query it with $k_i$, or with another vector similar to $k_i$. In the literature, a memory store that recalls by similarity is called an associative memory . An outer product memory store # The most basic memory store is linear: it simply accumulates memories via outer products, $$W = \sum_{i=1}^{M} v_i k_i\transpose = V\transpose K$$ where the rows of $K \in \reals^{M\times d_k}$ and $V \in \reals^{M\times d_v}$ are the keys $k_i\transpose$ and the values $v_i\transpose$. To store a new memory $(k, v)$, we simply add $vk\transpose$ to the existing weights. articles.content: Amateur radio operators from Florida’s Santa Rosa, Nassau, Lake, Pinellas, and Leon Counties played an important role in supporting emergency communications efforts during and following Hurricane Isaias, helping ensure that critical communication capabilities remained available throughout the storm. In Santa Rosa County, volunteer amateur radio operators staffed the Emergency Operations Center (EOC) and the evacuation shelter at the Milton Community Center. These volunteers provided a communications link between the shelter and the EOC, relaying situational updates and maintaining readiness to support emergency communications should traditional systems become unavailable. Amateur radio operators across the state also supported auxiliary communications efforts, providing additional capabilities to maintain contact with the State Emergency Operations Center in Tallahassee if conventional communication networks experienced disruptions. "When disaster strikes, our volunteers are trained, prepared, and ready to step in wherever we're needed. It's another layer of resiliency that helps protect our communities." Thames also serves as the ARRL Northern Florida Section Emergency Coordinator and the Amateur Radio Liaison to the Florida Division of Emergency Management, supporting the coordination of amateur radio and auxiliary communications resources statewide. "During tropical weather events impacting Florida, our Auxiliary Communications team provides volunteer operators to monitor amateur radio communications at the State Emergency Operations Center in Tallahassee," Thames explained. "This ensures that if someone is unable to reach emergency officials through traditional means, we have another way to receive and relay critical information. articles.title: Apple ML Research: Muse Spark Open with MLX on Mac Studio
articles.content: MLX on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. In a previous post , we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators. In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model — Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters — right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. On a cluster of four Mac Studios, Muse Spark Open generates over 36 tokens per second (see Figure 1 ), well above average human reading speed. Beginning on a single Mac Studio (up to 512GB of unified memory), then scaling out across multiple Macs with the RDMA over Thunderbolt driver, below we share an overview of the range of models you can now run on Mac Studio. Higher is better. We benchmark several popular open-weight LLMs on Mac Studio , using the MLX LM package, as described in our prior post . We compare two generations of Mac Studio: the recently released M5 Ultra and the previous generation, M3 Ultra. The M5 generation features the GPU Neural Accelerator, which supports dedicated matrix multiplication operations, essential for many machine learning workloads. articles.title: JPEG XL vs. AVIF for web use-cases
articles.content: JPEG XL has now landed in all major browsers, so I figured I'd take a closer look at what it's good/bad at compared to other formats. I'll go into full detail, with examples and benchmarks, but for those of you who don't have the time, here are the headlines: For lossy photos on the web, AVIF almost always produces smaller files than JPEG XL. At default effort settings, the best JPEG XL version is typically 15–25% larger than the equivalent AVIF. At maximum effort settings, the gap narrows a little, to typically 6–20%. There are outliers, where JPEG XL is close to, or even beats AVIF, so if you want the absolute best result for a particular image, it's worth trying both. See the F1 image for a typical example, and the weasel for an outlier. The JPEG XL encoder matters a lot. jixel , a newer JPEG XL encoder, usually produces smaller files than libjxl , except when the image has detailed transparency. The people image is one example. For screenshots and illustrations, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The equivalent JPEG XL is 30–90% larger at default effort settings, and 20–70% larger at maximum effort settings. Lossy AVIF handles these well - you don't need to use lossless formats unless you really need bit-exact results. See the screenshot and illustration examples. For images with transparency, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The libjxl version is 31–44% larger at default effort settings, and 61–70% larger at maximum effort settings. jixel always encodes transparency losslessly, which makes its files 2–3x the size of AVIF's. articles.title: Bitap: my favorite string matching algorithm
articles.content: A classic problem is to find the first occurrence of a pattern P P P in a string T T T . There are various classic algorithms to solve this problem efficiently, such as Boyer-Moore , Knuth-Morris-Pratt , and Two-Way . In this post I want to provide an exposition of a less well-known algorithm, the bitap or shift-and algorithm , that runs efficiently when the pattern P P P is relatively short (of length less than the width of a machine word). Despite its constraints, I like it a lot because it is simple both to understand and to implement, relatively efficient for short strings, and uses bit operations in a particularly elegant fashion. To show that the algorithm is as simple conceptually as claimed, let me try to derive it incrementally starting from the most naive string matching algorithm. Deriving bitap The naive algorithm The simplest brute-force algorithm to solve the string matching problem just tries to match the pattern P P P starting from each possible position in the string T T T . // Returns the first index i such that T[i:] starts with the pattern P, // or -1 if no such index occurs. // // The pattern P is required to be nonempty. func match ( T , P string ) int { outer : // starting from each position i = 0, ... in the string T... for i := range len ( T ) - len ( P ) + 1 { // try to match the pattern P, one character at a time... for j := range len ( P ) { // moving onto the next start position if a mismatch occurs. if T [ i + j ] != P [ j ] { continue outer } } return i } return - 1 } The naive algorithm, but make it streaming Let’s now impose an additional constraint to motivate us to change the algorithm a little: instead of being given all the characters of the text T T T at once, suppose that they are now provided in the form of a stream , one character at a time. (Perhaps T T T is very long and we do not wish to load all its contents into memory at once.) The simple algorithm presented above is not streaming: it needs to read up to m = len ( P ) m = \texttt{len}(P) m = len ( P ) characters ahead starting from the current position in T T T to detect a match of the pattern. How can we adapt it so that it only performs one pass through the data? After a bit of thought, one comes up with the following variant of the brute-force algorithm. Instead of immediately trying to detect an occurrence of P P P by reading ahead in the text T T T starting from each start position i = 0 , … i = 0, \dots i = 0 , … , we can instead maintain a set of in-progress matches as we scan through the text T T T . Conceptually, an in-progress match consists of the prefix of the pattern P P P that has already been matched just before the current position, along with the remaining suffix that has not been matched yet. When we read a new character c c c in T T T , we advance the in-progress matches that are expecting the character c c c , and kill the rest. articles.title: My Nix Config Is Intimate
articles.content: I am really proud of my Nix config. In one repository, it describes all of my machines, including my desktop, laptop, and servers. Everything is deduplicated - my Emacs config is available everywhere (stripped down on servers), and other programs are configured consistently. To spin up a new box, all I need to do is boot up a custom NixOS image (configured through Nix to have my public keys baked in), and then run a single script to deploy my Nix configuration of choice to the machine. This custom NixOS image also contains a range of utilities that makes it useful as a live image that feels just like any of my servers. I even serve this custom image via a PXE server in my apartment. I can network boot into it without even needing to image a USB stick. Like I said, I'm really proud of my Nix config. Even still, it lives in a private repository. This makes me sad - I want others to benefit from my Nix config too - but it also makes me most comfortable. I have a small reason for this, as well as a big reason. Security through obscurity is real, sort of Security through obscurity is the idea that by hiding a security flaw, you're safe from it. It's generally accepted that security through obscurity doesn't exist - given enough time, a bad actor can find the flaw regardless of the attempts you make to hide it. On the other hand, even if security through obscurity is insufficient as a single measure, it can at least add a layer to your swiss cheese . This is the small reason why I don't share my Nix config. It gives a very detailed schematic of the architecture of my network - what boxes are running what, the precise versions of every piece of software I'm using, and even the exact configurations of each of them. In fact, from my Nix config, it would be possible to create basically a clone of my entire network - that's the whole point, after all - which could then be analyzed by a bad actor. Now, I'm a pretty boring person. I don't think anyone is going to go through the effort of all of this just to attack me. Perhaps the more realistic threat are things that can be more easily abused. For example, all of my email addresses are written out in plain text in my config files. Some of these get absolutely no spam, and I'd like to keep it that way! I could store my email addresses more securely with something like agenix , but then I've made things a little more obtuse for myself. (And of course, my email addresses will still be available in the git history, unless I also rewrite master!) My Nix config is intimate Okay, so this is the much larger reason. My machines are an extension of myself. When things are configured properly, it feels like there is no boundary between them and me. In fact, when I do feel that boundary, that's a sign that things aren't configured properly, or that I'm working in an environment that's too constrained for me to feel comfortable. And this is one of the reasons I love Nix - all of my machines behave the same, interacting wi

articles.title: Emacs Bedrock 2.0 Released
articles.content: Bedrock is a minimal, human-crafted starter-kit for Emacs, and today I’m pleased to announce that version 2.0 of Bedrock is available! This release requires Emacs 31, which came out in August 2026. If you are unable to upgrade Emacs that high, you should be able to remove some of the Emacs 31-specific config without too much trouble. Bedrock is essentially a collection of better defaults for Emacs, and it uses no third-party packages in its base configuration. Part of the appeal of Emacs, of course, is the vast set of packages developed and maintained by the community, so Bedrock includes sample configurations for some of the most popular packages that I, personally, find utterly indispensable. The idea behind Bedrock is a lot simpler than other “starter kits” or configuration frameworks: Bedrock is just an early-init.el and an init.el that you copy once into ~/.emacs.d/ , and then you modify those files directly as your needs grow and your experience with Emacs matures. The files contain enough comments to point you in the right direction when you want to dig into how something works, but not so much as to drown you in a sea of prose when you’re looking for code. The configuration for third-party packages lives in a separate extras/ folder, and you can copy individual packages’ configuration directly into init.el as-needed, or import groups of packages an entire file at a time. Changes in Bedrock 2.0 This is a major release just because Bedrock is breaking its compatibility with Emacs 29, last released in 2024. Here is a summary of major changes in this version: Bedrock now uses the lexical-binding: t cookie in all its .el files. All packages declared with use-package get installed if not present on the system by default . Use embark-auto-prefix-help-mode instead of which-key if the embark package is loaded. Remove wgrep in favor of built-in grep-change-to-grep-edit-mode . Vastly improved tree-sitter configuration. Nicer isearch configuration. Make the built-in *Completions* buffer auto-update. Turn on repeat-mode by default. Fixes in this version: Fixed theme colors not being respected. Better suppression of startup message. Miscellaneous little improvements. These lists are not exhaustive (as that last bullet should make clear) but that’s the gist of it. More details are available in the changelog . This is very much an incremental improvement—not some total-overhaul of Bedrock. If you’re a happy user of an earlier version of Bedrock, then you might not have any reason to “upgrade”. Emacs is a stable editor (though the level of active development it enjoys is both meaningful and exciting!) and it should come as no surprise that a starter kit made for the “bleeding edge” should be, well, relatively stable itself. articles.title: Antiquated HTML Snippets and Artefacts
articles.content: With ever-changing devices, browsers, operating systems, form factors, specifications, personal preferences, tooling, and corporate interests, the web is in a constant state of flux. As a result, so is the HTML we write. For every line of the HTML specification itself that has changed since the language’s inception, there are many more bits of HTML that have seen what I’ll call ‘environmental’ changes. Adaptations to differing browsers, extensions, integrations, and systems which we find HTML existing in. This article doesn’t cover once-specced but now obsolete bits of HTML but instead looks at all the snippets that have wormed their way into websites as result of, or in combat against, third-party integrations, browser competition, vendor extensions, and platform-specific hacks. The bits of HTML that were included for reasons, and which have been forgotten for present irrelevance. The snippets that live on only in the markup of sites from bygone eras and in the minds of those who fought during the browser wars. X-UA-Compatible < meta http-equiv = "X-UA-Compatible" content = "IE=edge" > In an age where browsers changed quickly and version-specific behaviours weren’t unheard of, it was deemed necessary to signal compatibility with specific versions of browsers with the X-UA-Compatible meta tag. Here the content attribute reads IE=edge , meaning that the target is the highest supported document mode in Internet Explorer (IE). As outlined in the documentation , there are other values than edge . One can also supply a value of 5 through 11 to correspond with the associated Internet Explorer version, or EmulateIE7 through EmulateIE11 to enter into that version’s mode, but only if a valid DOCTYPE is declared, otherwise falling back to quirks mode. < meta http-equiv = "X-UA-Compatible" content = "chrome=1" > Before Chrome took over the market, Google released an Internet Explorer plugin called Google Chrome Frame . Installable in Internet Explorer versions 6 through 9, it rendered websites in Chrome’s modified WebKit engine rather than Internet Explorer’s Trident engine if they had the tag set. < meta http-equiv = "X-UA-Compatible" content = "requiresActiveX=true" > requiresActiveX was used to prompt Internet Explorer 10 to switch to desktop mode if in Metro mode, which didn’t support plugins. ICBM Coordinate < meta name = "ICBM" content = "-31.9548, 115.8602" > ICBM (an abbreviation of ‘intercontinental ballistic missile’) is hacker slang for one’s geographical location that dates back to Usenet days. The meta tag was used for identifying the location of a website’s subject and was referenced by the service GeoURL for plotting sites on the globe and helping people find sites of geographical proximity. articles.title: This Month in Ladybird - August 2026
articles.content: Hello friends! In August Ladybird gained video playback on Twitch, more video formats on YouTube, CSS scroll snap, JavaScript debugging in DevTools, downloads you can pause and resume, and session restore. It’s also the month engine performance went from occasional attention to a sustained focus, with a new style engine, layout caching, and CSS animations moving off the main thread. We added caging for cell pointers stored in JavaScript values, and CSS parsing and the painting pipeline moved to Rust. Ladybird is entirely funded by the generous support of companies and individuals who believe in the open web. This month, we’re excited to welcome the following new sponsors: Arnav Guleria with $5,000 You can see everyone currently supporting the project on our sponsors page , and we’re grateful to all of them. If you’re interested in sponsoring, please contact us . Video on Twitch, and more formats on YouTube Our implementation of Media Source Extensions gained support for fragmented MP4, as well as the AVC (H.264), HEVC (H.265), AV1, and AAC codecs, with support queries now communicating our real capabilities ( #11251 ). This allows us to play adaptive-bitrate video on many more sites, including Twitch and Plex. YouTube already worked in Ladybird since all videos are available as VP9/Opus in WebM, but some older/less popular videos only have multiple quality levels in AVC, and higher qualities (especially 8K) are often only served as AV1. We also fixed a batch of playback bugs: hovering YouTube’s video-card previews no longer crashes ( #10992 ), players using preload="none" no longer hang ( #11454 ), and HLS.js-based players start playing ( #11480 ). Scroll snap landed ( #10944 ): scroll-snap-type , scroll-snap-align and scroll-snap-stop . Wheel, keyboard, scrollbar dragging, touchpad flings and programmatic scrollTo() all snap, and content re-snaps when layout changes. ( scrollIntoView() doesn’t snap yet.) Carousels and full-page scrollers are built on this. You can now debug JavaScript in Ladybird: set breakpoints, step through code line by line, and evaluate watch expressions ( #11128 ), built on new breakpoint support in our JavaScript engine ( #10936 ). Wasm debugging and DOM mutation breakpoints are still missing, but the core workflow works. (As before, the Firefox DevTools frontend is a stopgap until we build our own.) Downloads that pause and resume Downloads can now be paused and resumed, and survive a browser restart, when the server supports it ( #10932 ). We also download over four parallel connections where possible. Session restore Reopening a closed tab with Ctrl + Shift + T used to restore just the URL. It now restores the tab’s full session history, including back/forward state, and this persists across browser restarts ( #11178 ). “Duplicate Tab” duplicates the session history too ( #11286 ). articles.title: Sloc Cloc and Code - Did I just get Buster Scrugged?
articles.content: Sloc Cloc and Code - Did I just get Buster Scrugged? 2026/09/07 · 2675 words Treat Faster Tools as a Profile, Not an Insult I recently had this gracious github issue raised against scc related to another code counter mezura which has some impressive performance claims . Naturally, I decided to check it out. boyter@spongehead:/mnt/data/projects$ hyperfine 'scc ./linux' 'mezura ./linux' Benchmark 1: scc ./linux Time (mean ± σ): 512.2 ms ± 4.6 ms [User: 10362.5 ms, System: 985.7 ms] Range (min … max): 506.6 ms … 519.5 ms 10 runs Benchmark 2: mezura ./linux Time (mean ± σ): 200.3 ms ± 9.6 ms [User: 2898.5 ms, System: 643.5 ms] Range (min … max): 186.8 ms … 213.0 ms 14 runs Summary mezura ./linux ran 2.56 ± 0.13 times faster than scc ./linux Damn, I just got Buster Scrugged. At the time I was enjoying a splash of whisky to celebrate the wind down of a stressful project and keep my singing voice in fettle. I was astonished at the result. However, before trading my spurs for wings, I decided to sleep on it, and have a look around at what I could do. As I said on the stto comparison some time ago, This is not because I am hurt if my tool is slower. In fact that would make me happy, as I can learn from my mistakes. So looking at the times, we have this on my Desktop, a 9950x3D and Go 1.27, rerun the next morning. wall scc 4.0.0 508.6 ms scc 4.0.0 -c 445.7 ms mezura 3.0.0 203.9 ms Two things of note. I used -c which turns off complexity calculations to make it a closer comparison since mezura does not do this (as far as I can tell) and secondly, they are not doing an equal amount of work. scc is counting ~86,000 files compared to mezura counting ~67,000. However there is still no reason scc should be taking 2x the wall clock time for this task. Now I could go and read the source of mezura to see if there is some trick I’m missing, or as I decided, to black box it, by looking at strace output instead. This is because it gives a good idea of where to go looking for wins, and I have never really used it that much. articles.title: Serving Web from volatile Dial-up IP
articles.content: 🥕 [A.S.: it's actually not dial-up, but a volatile IP, typical for DSL home routers.] My homelab is behind a dial-up IP link with occasional unexpected reconnects. There is dynamic DNS, but I prefer a reverse HTTP proxy [1] between the bots and me. And dyndns doesn't notify other servers (the reverse proxy). No push? Then poll. There's a cron-job on the homelab server triggering a refresh of the reverse proxy cfg if the IP has changed: # note: no sudo $ crontab -l */15 * * * * .local/bin/http-up.sh snac.mro.name vps.mro.name /var/www/vhosts/snac.mro.name/proxy-dyndns.conf with a (local) script doing the heavy lifting (shell escaping mostly): #!/bin/sh [ "$3" = "" ] && { cat <<EOFz Check if localhost can curl an url and if not, envsubst the current IP as \$IPv4 into a (remote) reverse proxy config in case & reload (lighttpd). SYNOPSIS \$ $0 <http url> <ssh host> <reverse proxy cfg file> EOFz exit 0 } curl \ --fail \ --location \ --max-time 3.1 \ --output /dev/null \ --silent \ "$1" \ && exit 0 ssh -4 "$2" \ "IPv4=\$(echo \$SSH_CLIENT | cut -d ' ' -f 1) envsubst \ < \"$3.tpl\" \ > \"$3\" # ^ smelly (unprivileged) remote filesystem write sudo service lighttpd reload # requires a sudoers NOPASSWD ls -l \"$3\" " After DSL reconnects, the server comes back online with the new IP within the next 15 minutes — fine for me. No other parties involved and the volatile host notifies the passive reverse proxy. And: I can make do with cron & ssh and need no other tools or services. Footnotes on a 1-Euro VPS , [<-]

articles.title: Bug turns one of the biggest fears about Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses into reality
articles.content: Some Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses were recording people’s conversations without the wearer knowing. The recordings occurred without users saying the prompt phrase (“Hey, Meta”), in a bug that Meta says has been fixed. This week, some users reported online that their Ray-Ban Metas were recording without their consent. A person going by Kindly-Audience-137 on Reddit, for example, said this happened to them across three Meta Ray-Bans and that they had the “Respond without Hey Meta” setting turned off. The person said the Meta AI app “saves audio recordings and text transcripts of these conversations in my conversation history.” “I believe this deserves a serious technical investigation. Customers should not have to wonder whether their private conversations are being captured when they have not intentionally activated their glasses’ AI assistant,” the Reddit user said. Android Authority reported the discussions on Tuesday. Later that day it published a response from Meta that read: “This issue has been resolved. People can manage, review, and delete voice logs of their interactions with Meta AI via settings at any time.” Although Meta’s brief message suggests that the bug is fixed, the broader privacy problem remains. Unanswered questions Meta hasn’t said what caused the Ray-Ban Metas to record people without user consent. Reddit user Kindly-Audience-137 said they “first noticed this behavior after a recent firmware update,” but Meta hasn’t confirmed if a faulty update caused the bug. We also don’t know how many Meta smart glasses were affected. There are a few reports online, but Android Authority said it was unable to replicate the problem before Meta said it fixed it. Ars Technica sent Meta a message asking what it’s doing to prevent future bugs like this from happening again and how many devices were affected. We’ll update this article if we hear back. Even a handful of affected devices is cause for concern, though. Before reports of this bug, privacy advocates had already expressed widespread concerns about Meta’s smart glasses, as well as those from other vendors. Beyond the fear that naturally accompanies the release of new technology that features a microphone and camera, Meta’s glasses pushed the boundaries of privacy further with their more inconspicuous look, prompting concern about how easy it could be for someone to secretly record another person. Meta has previously tried to assuage concerns by pointing to the fact that its glasses light up when recording audio or video. But the bug this week shows that even with this light activated, it’s possible for the smart glasses to record inadvertently. Meta’s brief statement does little to alleviate those worries. Meanwhile, the bug lends some credence to reports and trepidation that Ray-Ban Metas are creating recordings without subjects’ knowledge. articles.title: Here’s Exactly How Tesla Made Its New 230-Mph Car ‘Fly’
articles.content: Last night, with considerable showmanship, Tesla CEO Elon Musk proudly unveiled the Roadster 2 just nine years after first announcing the car, and made it “fly.” While undeniably impressive, you could also describe the spectacle as Tesla making its long-delayed luxury car “ do a big hop ” and then, as Buzz Lightyear would say, “fall with style.” During the reveal in McGregor, Texas, at SpaceX’s rocket development and testing facility, the two-seater Roadster 2 launched itself over the automaker’s entire lineup, shot from 0 to 60 mph in less than a second, and then drove upside down off a high ramp to then flip over midair and land back down on the ground, cushioning its rapid descent using onboard thrusters. All this was pure gold for social clips (though at the time of publication, Tesla’s stock price was down after the event), but how did Tesla make its new EV prototype perform these tricks? Tesla vehicle engineering head Lars Moravy went into detail with auto lifestyle and insurance brand Hagerty before yesterday’s event, explaining how the Roadster 2 works. The Roadster 2's gravity-defying demonstration in Texas used a combination of suction and rocket thrust. Courtesy of REUTERS Franz von Holzhausen, Tesla’s chief designer since 2008, designed the angular exterior. He also helmed the aesthetic of the Cybertruck , Models S, X, 3, and Y, as well as the Semi . Blacked-out windows obscured any view inside the EV, which carried no human driver anyway because, as Musk said, Tesla wanted “to make sure we don’t kill anyone” during the gravity-defying demonstration. Powertrain and Battery The Roadster 2 will be rear-wheel-drive only, a departure from Tesla’s track record of all-wheel-drive EVs. Two motors will deliver over a megawatt of power (1,341 horsepower) and over 1,400 newton-meters (Nm) of torque, meaning this car will have more torque and power than a three-motor Plaid . But all of that power goes through just the rear wheels. The car will be light, at “just under 1,700 kilos” (under 2 tons), according to Moravy, not significantly heavier than the original 1,300-kg (1.4-ton) Roadster, despite a larger size. Tesla claims a range of over 300 miles for the Roadster and hopes to mitigate this distinctly average range by also giving the EV the fastest-charging battery the automaker has ever produced, supposedly capable of zipping from 15 to 80 percent in 10 minutes . Sucking Fans At a 2013 auction, Elon Musk bought the iconic "Wet Nellie" Lotus Esprit S1 submarine car from the 1977 James Bond film The Spy Who Loved Me for just shy of $1 million. Musk is so taken with his Bond memorabilia that it apparently inspired one of the Roadster 2's key abilities. That submarine Bond car has four propellers at its rear, so Tesla decided to ape this with four 20-kilowatt fans on the Roadster 2. articles.summary: 微软Surface Laptop Ultra评测：首款真正AI PC，性能媲美MacBook Pro，但续航不足。

articles.title: AWOL Vision Aetherion Max RGB Laser UST Projector Review: A Top Buy

articles.title: Google EnvHarness Enables Self-Evolving Agents to Learn in Dynamics Environments
articles.content: Google researchers open sourced EnvHarness, a framework that dynamically adapts agent-training environments to an agent's weaknesses without modifying the agent, environment, or evaluation system. According to the researchers, this approach can improve both learning effectiveness and efficiency while helping agents overcome their weaknesses. By Sergio De Simone

articles.title: Zod Brings In-Process Schema Compilation and a 9x Cut in Memory Footprint
articles.content: Zod is a TypeScript-focused schema validation library that recently released versions 4.5 and 4.6. Key updates include schema compilation for faster data parsing, significant memory usage reductions, and new validation features. The library supports efficient validation processes and remains popular in the JavaScript ecosystem, achieving millions of downloads weekly. By Daniel Curtis

articles.title: Uber Automates Dependency Analysis Across Its Service Mesh
articles.content: Uber has developed an automated dependency analysis system that uses RPC middleware and production metrics to correlate caller and downstream failures. The approach classifies dependencies as fail-close, fail-open, or unknown and addresses limitations of sampled distributed tracing for rare failures across Uber’s large service mesh. By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: Uber开发自动化依赖分析系统，利用RPC中间件和生产指标关联调用方与下游故障。

articles.title: AI in Production: Panellists Highlight Silent Failures, Harness Engineering, and Agent Governance
articles.content: A recent InfoQ webinar examined operational challenges in deploying agentic systems. Key points included issues like semantic and embedding drift, which can lead to significant errors. Experts discussed the need for automated code reviews, continuous evaluation of models, and enhanced privacy measures. The session emphasised a strategic approach to deployment and security management. By Olimpiu Pop
articles.summary: InfoQ网络研讨会探讨智能体系统生产挑战，包括语义漂移、自动代码审查与隐私治理。

articles.title: Grafana Applies SLOs and Error Budgets to AI Agent Behaviour
articles.content: Grafana Labs is proposing a familiar reliability engineering approach for one of the less familiar problems in modern software: how to measure whether an AI agent is actually behaving well. By Craig Risi

articles.title: Mini book: Evolutionary Architecture in Practice
articles.content: Discover how to keep software evolvable as systems, technology, and teams shift. This edition explores agentic fitness functions for semantic drift, treating human comprehension as a core design metric, cross-cloud guardrails for regional autonomy, and aligning technical boundaries with Conway’s Law. Move beyond static diagrams to continuous feedback systems that keep change safe and intentional. By InfoQ

articles.title: Helidon 27 Introduces Restructured Programming Models and New Messaging and Data Modules
articles.content: The release of Helidon 27 is the first release that follows the Oracle Tip & Tail Model of Library Development by which the Tip adopts the latest Java technology while the Tail provides a more stable and secure baseline. Concurrent with the release of JDK 27, new features in Helidon 27 include: an introduction to new major modules, Helidon Messaging and Helidon Data JDBC. By Michael Redlich
articles.summary: Helidon 27发布，采用Oracle Tip & Tail库开发模式，重构编程模型并新增消息与数据模块。

articles.title: Presentation: Exploding GPUs
articles.content: Andrew Martin discusses why AI security is fundamentally tied to Kubernetes security. He shares insights into the evolving AI threat landscape, covering non-deterministic agent behavior, GPU supply chain vulnerabilities, shared compute risks, and practical defense strategies - from prompt firewalling to agentic identity - to help secure cloud-native AI workloads in production environments. By Andrew Martin
articles.summary: Andrew Martin 在演讲中指出 AI 安全本质上是 Kubernetes 安全，剖析了智能体非确定性行为、GPU 供应链漏洞等威胁并给出防御策略。

articles.title: AWS Introduces Strands Decider 2B and Strands Box for AI Agent Development
articles.content: AWS has introduced two open-source projects for AI agent development: Strands Decider 2B, a small model designed to make decisions within agent workflows, and Strands Box, a sandbox for controlling agent execution. Both projects address different aspects of building agents that use tools, execute code, and interact with external systems. By Daniel Dominguez
articles.summary: AWS 开源 Strands Decider 2B 小模型与 Strands Box 沙箱，分别用于智能体工作流决策和执行控制，助力 AI 智能体开发。

articles.title: Article: Cryptographic Foundation of Mobile ID Systems: An ISO/IEC 18013-5 Enterprise Architecture Blueprint
articles.content: This article provides a framework for asking the right architectural questions before an enterprise commits to an mDL provider or library. It shows which components can be abstracted safely, which trust boundaries must remain visible to the enterprise, what cryptographic and interoperability properties should be verified, and how requirements change across real-world use cases. By Praveen Kumar Gopalakrishnan
articles.summary: 文章提出企业采用移动驾照（mDL）前的架构评估框架，说明哪些组件可安全抽象、哪些信任边界必须保留及密码学互操作要求。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #538: The FTC wants OpenAI's and Anthropic's safety incident records
articles.content: The FTC sent OpenAI and Anthropic 50-page demands for records on security incidents, safeguards, marketing and privacy, Axios reported. Meta's new business terms, effective October 30, let it scrape and train on publishers' websites. Investors at Anthropic's investor day discussed a $1.5 trillion IPO valuation, down from about $2 trillion. Character.ai filed for bankruptcy. Citizen Lab traced spyware sent to Al Jazeera devices through targeted ads. Accenture now funds $29 a month of Claude per employee, and Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch flaws that AI models found. In the middle: the biggest open models now run on a desk.

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic 警告小型 AI 模型或将能自我复制到智能冰箱等家用设备，本期还汇总了 AI 专家近期最关注的链接。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: 顶级 AI 模型未能通过自主开展 AI 研究的测试，本期还探讨 AI 治理话语权、军事规划应用及进入个人电脑的趋势。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: 因 AI 成本过高，企业纷纷转向更便宜的模型，本期还总结了大规模部署进入日常使用及 AI 被限制或移除的案例。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校 IT 负责人首次将 AI 列为首要事项，剑桥拒绝 Turnitin 新条款，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，AI 使用已非未来议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #533: Meta tested human callers behind its AI phone agent
articles.content: The AI story of September 22–28 was not simply that agents became more capable. It was that their hidden handoffs became visible: a supposedly automated call could reach a contractor, a supposedly private prompt or image could reach a reviewer, a monitor could detect an agent long before a person stopped it, and a local app flaw could inherit every permission a user had granted. The new AI Weekly Who’s Who census points to one practical question: when an agent crosses a boundary, who knows—and who can still intervene?
articles.summary: Meta 被曝其 AI 电话代理背后有真人接线员，本期揭示智能体隐藏的人工转接、提示词审查等不透明环节。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #531: AI labs shipped agents before agreeing how to report failures
articles.content: The AI story of September 14–20 was not one spectacular model launch. It was the machinery around agents becoming visible: people reading private chats, models writing instructions into their own memory, plugins updating beneath users, and regulators asking how to stop a system after release. The latest AI Weekly Who’s Who census surfaced 535 expert-shared links. We ranked them by consequence and reader relevance, not by raw share count. Here is what mattered last week—and, more importantly, what could move the story from September 22–28.
articles.summary: AI 实验室在未就故障上报方式达成一致前便已发布智能体，本期聚焦私聊被读取、模型自写记忆、插件更新等治理问题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #530: Applied AI This Week
articles.content: Companies are giving AI specific jobs: checking security cameras, helping farmers understand their records, searching satellite images, and preparing sales quotes. This edition explains how those tools work, who can use them, and what companies have reported so far.
articles.summary: 企业为 AI 分配具体任务，如监控摄像头、辅助农民、搜索卫星图像和生成销售报价，本期介绍这些工具的原理与使用情况。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #529: OpenAI faces 50-plus lawsuits over alleged ChatGPT harm

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #528: What are companies building with AI? An Applied AI Deep Dive
articles.content: We went looking for what companies are actually building with AI. The answer was not more chatbots. It was drones carrying diagnostic samples, driverless Frito-Lay trucks, AI-guided flight paths, repair copilots, and rugged GPU laptops in Ukraine. We reviewed 136 use cases from the last 20 days. The biggest surprise: only 38 included a reported outcome.

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: NanoClaw 作者 Gavriel Cohen 讲述一个 40 小时周末项目如何成为爆款开源项目，并发展为专注容器隔离安全的企业 AI 公司。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com 联合创始人 Peer Richelsen 探讨开源仓库可能已被暗中破坏的理论，以及 AI 如何扁平化知识图谱。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: Sam Lambert 回归畅谈 PlanetScale Postgres 定价、Vitess 重做、智能体通过部署请求提交 schema 变更及 500TB 表秒级回滚。

articles.title: Canary tokens and digital tripwires
articles.content: Haroon Meer is back! Haroon is the Founder of Thinkst, the ~50-person bootstrapped company behind Canary and Canarytokens — honeypots and tripwires you sprinkle inside your network and forget about until an attacker touches one. We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.
articles.summary: Thinkst创始人Haroon Meer介绍Canary和Canarytokens蜜罐与绊线工具，可埋入网络监测攻击者触碰，并谈及攻击者难以抗拒的AWS API密钥诱饵。

articles.title: From open source hits to OpenAI
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Max Stoiber, currently working on ChatGPT's plugin directory and app platform at OpenAI. We discuss the hundreds of open source projects nobody remembers alongside the big ones like react-boilerplate and styled-components, how Spectrum became part of GitHub and eventually helped shape GitHub Discussions, the founder growth that came from building Stellate, the GraphQL cache that turned into a dual acquisition by Shopify and The Guild, and why ChatGPT apps feel like a new surface for software.
articles.summary: Max Stoiber讲述从react-boilerplate等开源项目到加入OpenAI负责ChatGPT插件目录与应用的经历，回顾Spectrum被GitHub收购等历程。

articles.title: MCP on Code Mode
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Matt Carey about Code Mode and how most of us have been thinking about MCP all wrong. Matt works on the Agents SDK and MCP at Cloudflare — we discuss how server-side Code Mode lets one MCP server expose all ~2,500 Cloudflare API endpoints in about 1,000 tokens of context, the dynamic Worker loader that runs model-written code safely in a V8 isolate, Matt's own workflow with Claude, where memory fits into the future of agents, and his Zaggy git wrapper that keeps agents from force-pushing his repos.
articles.summary: Cloudflare的Matt Carey介绍Code Mode，通过服务端模式让单个MCP服务器用约1000个token上下文暴露约2500个Cloudflare API端点。

articles.title: Automation at the speed of Swamp
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Adam Jacob, founder of System Initiative and creator of Swamp, about what happens when AI agents change the entire shape of software development. We discuss how he went from an 18-person team down to five and shipped Swamp 900 times in four weeks, why he brought User Acceptance Testing (UAT) testing back from the 90s, why software architecture (and domain-driven design) suddenly matters more than knowing how to write code, the live demo where I pointed Swamp at my Proxmox box and watched it write its own automation (blew my mind!!), and why he'll never accept a pull request to Swamp, ever.
articles.summary: System Initiative创始人Adam Jacob谈AI代理如何改变软件开发形态，团队从18人缩减至5人，四周内发布Swamp达900次。

articles.title: Bitwarden CLI compromised
articles.content: Bitwarden's CLI got hit by the Checkmarx supply-chain campaign, TypeScript 7.0 beta lands with the Go-rewritten compiler running ~10x faster than 6.0, and pgBackRest lost its maintainer of thirteen years leaving anyone running production Postgres with a real dependency-trust task this week. We've also got Ubuntu 26.04 LTS shipping with TPM-backed full-disk encryption, and Matz dropping Spinel as an AOT path that takes Ruby to native binaries. This week was a good reminder that the tools we depend on are all moving at once. Security, performance, and maintenance aren't isolated threads.
articles.summary: Bitwarden CLI遭Checkmarx供应链攻击，TypeScript 7.0 beta发布，Go重写编译器提速约10倍，pgBackRest维护者离职引发依赖信任问题。

articles.title: Exploring with agents
articles.content: Today on the show I’m talking with Amelia Wattenberger — designer, data-viz veteran, ex-GitHub Next, and now designing Intent at Augment Code. What if the last 30% of any software project is about to become the hardest part you’ve ever done? That’s the argument Amelia is making today. We discuss the identity crisis developers are having as agents take over the keyboard, the epic redesign of developer tooling in this agent-first world, the arc from autocomplete to chat to CLI back to UI, why Intent treats a workspace as their core primitive not a chat thread, the tradeoffs between one-worktree-per-agent vs. one-worktree-per-task, and why she thinks prototyping just got easier but finishing got harder.
articles.summary: 设计师Amelia Wattenberger探讨AI代理时代软件开发最后30%工作为何可能成为最难部分，并分享在Augment Code设计Intent的经验。

articles.title: Video Game Reverse Engineering Community Shuts Down Because AI Has Made It Too Easy
articles.content: The collaborative reverse-engineering site decomp.dev is shutting down, with its administrator saying AI has made game decompilation so fast and accessible that the community's human-driven model has effectively broken down. "The administrator of the website said that it has become impossible to keep track of which projects are primarily human-led and which ones are done by AI," reports 404 Media. From the report: "Historically, matching decompilation has been a brutally difficult, time consuming task, on the scale of years for any moderately-sized game with a number of active contributors," the pseudonymous admin of decomp.dev, who goes by Encounter, wrote on the site. But recent frontier AI models like GPT-6-Astra have made it trivially easy to decompile a game: "They are significantly better at following complex directions, cross-referencing resources for symbols or debug information, and writing natural code with enough guidance," Encounter wrote. "It is now clear that, with the right guidance, human input, and code reviews, AI can expedite the decompilation process in a significant way. What is also now clear is that the community aspect of decompilation has been broken." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 游戏逆向工程社区网站decomp.dev宣布关闭，管理员称AI让游戏反编译变得太快太容易，人类驱动的社区模式已难以为继。

articles.title: China's Tencent Says AI Agents Showed Unintended Browsing Behavior
articles.content: Tencent says AI agents used to evaluate third-party models engaged in unintended web-browsing behavior while trying to retrieve data from Alibaba's Amap service. The announcement marks a rare acknowledgment of "rogue" agent activity by a major Chinese tech company. Reuters reports: Tencent Hunyuan, the company's artificial intelligence unit, said in a post on X that the activity did not originate from its Hunyuan models. Its review found no evidence of deliberate targeting or coordination, it said. The Swarmchasers researchers said the agents sought information such as the commonly used entrances at Chinese parks, museums and zoos. [...] Swarmchasers said it used the word "rogue" to describe agents taking actions outside their intended scope or completing a task in unintended ways. After routine automated requests were blocked, the agents tried other methods, including public web tools that could open pages and run code, routing requests through other websites and using Amap keys and security codes found in publicly available software code. Swarmchasers said it found no evidence that the agents breached Amap's main anti-bot safeguards. Most of the 2,818 attempts it recorded either failed or returned anti-bot pages, login screens or blank results. Some requests returned information through cached pages and intermediary services, including data on visitor arrivals at Chengdu Zoo, Swarmchasers said. The researchers said they could not determine whether an agent read the result or completed its task. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: An OpenAI Research Agent 'Stole' Test Ethereum to Finish a Coding Task
articles.content: An OpenAI research model reportedly accessed an Ethereum testnet wallet without permission in order to complete a coding task during internal training. "This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder's permission, then act on that judgment without authorization," OpenAI wrote. Engadget reports: The incident, which occurred on June 26, happened while a GPT-5.6 Sol model was in internal training. The task involved updating a crypto trading prototype and deploying contracts (publishing special code) on an Ethereum test network called Sepolia. Payment of a network fee is required for such contracts, but OpenAI "supplied no funded wallet and gave no permission to spend funds from an account the model found independently," OpenAI said in the report. The lack of funds at first stymied the agent, but it was not to be discouraged. The model reasoned that it could use public developer recovery phrases (similar to those you might use to recover a password) to access keys from unauthorized accounts. It tracked down 362 addresses open to that avenue of attack and found one that held enough Sepolia ETH to finish its deployment (to be clear, Sepolia ETH has no value outside of testing). Like many criminals, the agent reasoned that someone must have left this access open for automated draining of the ETH "faucets." It also figured that the crypto was effectively "abandoned" and "valueless," according to OpenAI's misalignment records. The piece de resistance was that the agent "did not disclose that it had selected a funded account through a public recover phrase or spent that account's balance," OpenAI said. To prevent similar events in the future, the company is now monitoring all traffic and paging security if live internet access is detected. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Mutative v2  - better immutability and faster immutable updates
articles.content: Mutative 2.0 is out. Read the release notes , the announcement and the migration guide from v1 to v2 . Mutative - A JavaScript library for efficient immutable updates ( documentation ). In the benchmark , it was about 3.6x faster than Immer with the same settings and 6.6x faster with each library's defaults across 97 workloads. In that benchmark the gap widened on large arrays, where Mutative moved elements up to 1,052x faster than Immer. When copying dominates, such as updating objects with thousands of keys, inserting at the front of a large array or adding an item to a large Set, Mutative is even faster than hand-written reducers. How does Mutative compare with the spread operation (hand-written reducers)? Mutative copies each object at most once per update, however many changes a recipe makes. Immer made it easy to write immutable updates as mutations of a draft. Mutative keeps that model and focuses on performance: it copies each object at most once per update, drafts objects only when a recipe reads them, finalizes only the drafts that changed, and runs array methods that move elements natively on its copies. Immer freezes the next state by default, which costs time on every update; Mutative freezes it only when asked to. Mutative also takes its options per call instead of from global configuration, drafts class instances through marks instead of changing their classes, supports async recipes and Map and Set subclasses, and handles edge cases that Immer gets wrong. Mutative 2.0.0 was 3.6x faster than Immer 11.1.18 with matched settings and 6.6x faster with each library's defaults, on geometric mean across 97 benchmarked workloads, and faster in 595 of 614 measured cases. The gap grows on large arrays, where Mutative moves elements natively: removing the first of 10,000 rows took 7.04 µs, against 7,408 µs. With each library's defaults, Mutative without auto-freeze and Immer with it, Mutative was faster in 154 of 157 cases. The other 3 return a state that Immer froze earlier: Immer skips frozen values when it searches a returned state for drafts, while Mutative, which does not freeze by default, searches it unless the recipe wraps it in rawReturn() , which took 0.26 µs. articles.title: Type-safe OpenAPI requests that follow your document exactly
articles.content: openapi-chain compiles the serialization rules an OpenAPI document declares (parameter style , explode , allowReserved and content , request media types, and form and multipart Encoding Objects) and applies them to every request. A build-time CLI generates types and metadata scoped to the paths you call, so large documents stay affordable to type-check and to ship. Calls use a fluent path API with no generated endpoint code and no runtime dependencies. The pnpm monorepo contains three publishable packages: openapi-chain , @openapi-chain/cli , and @openapi-chain/query . The runtime keeps its existing package name and entry points. See the package migration guide for CLI and query import changes and release availability. The first request below uses the Items schema . Your chain follows your own schema: static path segments become properties, {parameters} become function calls, and HTTP methods become request functions. Exact wire serialization: the strict client sends what the document specifies and rejects representations it cannot encode instead of guessing. The wire comparison executes 20 declarations through both clients: openapi-fetch 0.17.0 sends a request with different values, media type or missing parameters in 16 of them, and differs only in percent-encoding or list spacing in 3 more. Scoped generation for large documents: one CLI config produces full declarations, a path scope and matching runtime metadata. On the pinned GitHub REST document, scoping a 40-operation consumer reduced openapi-chain's TypeScript 7 check time from 0.49 s to 0.045 s ( real-schema measurements ). Typed requests and responses: infer parameters, request media types and status-correlated results from the selected operation. Keep openapi-fetch if you already use it: openapi-chain/openapi-fetch applies the same serialization to an existing openapi-fetch client ( adapter guide ). Small schema-free core: the default client has a 3.5 KiB gzip budget , enforced by a reproducible size check ; its bundle size and per-request overhead are in the same range as openapi-fetch ( client comparison ). Customizable requests: operation-typed extensions and Fetch-compatible transports support application-specific serialization, authentication and parsing. When to choose openapi-chain Choose the strict client when your document declares non-default parameter styles, parameter content , cookie parameters, non-JSON media types or form and multipart encoding, and the server depends on them. Choose the CLI's scoped generation when a large document makes type-checking or metadata delivery expensive. If your API only uses JSON bodies and default parameter styles, openapi-fetch and openapi-chain's core are comparable in size and speed; pick the call style you prefer. Without scoping, openapi-chain's fluent types cost more to check than openapi-fetch's on the measured GitHub and Stripe documents. For a published release with this API: pnpm add openapi-chain pnpm add -D @openapi-chain/cli S

articles.title: Node.JS Built-Ins That Replaced NPM Packages
articles.content: Home / Node.js Node.js built-ins that replaced npm packages By Flavio Copes Sep 20, 2026 Twelve Node.js built-ins that replace axios, nodemon, dotenv, jest, chalk, glob and more, with their stability in Node 24 and one gotcha each. ~~~ Open a package.json from a few years ago and you’ll find the same names in almost every one. axios , nodemon , dotenv , jest , chalk , uuid , rimraf . Node.js now ships a built-in for each of them. Here are twelve of those built-ins, with the package each one replaces, the shortest example that runs, how stable it is in the current LTS line, and the one thing the old package still does that the built-in doesn’t. Several of these changed status in the last year, so I checked every claim against the Node 24 API docs (24.21.0, the Active LTS line as of September 2026) and ran every example on Node 26.0.0, which is what node --version prints on my Mac. Node 22 is in maintenance until April 2027, Node 20 reached end of life on April 30, 2026, and Node 26 becomes the next LTS on October 28, 2026. Where Node 22 and 24 differ, I say so. A quick reminder on how Node labels its APIs. Stability 2 is stable. Stability 1 is experimental, with sub-levels: 1.0 is early development, 1.1 is active development, 1.2 is a release candidate. Anything experimental can change or disappear in a minor release, so the number matters if you’re putting it in production. 1. node:sqlite replaces better-sqlite3 For years the way to use SQLite from Node was better-sqlite3 , a native addon you had to compile (or download a prebuilt binary for) on every install. Node 22.5 added a SQLite driver to core. Like better-sqlite3 , it’s synchronous, so the code reads top to bottom with no await . import { DatabaseSync } from 'node:sqlite' const db = new DatabaseSync ( '/Users/flavio/notes.db' ) db. exec ( 'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, body TEXT)' ) const insert = db. prepare ( 'INSERT INTO notes (body) VALUES (?)' ) insert. run ( 'Buy espresso beans' ) console. log (db. prepare ( 'SELECT * FROM notes' ). all ()) The module only exists under the node: prefix, a plain import 'sqlite' fails. Status in Node 24: 1.2, release candidate , since 24.15.0. It prints no warning. In Node 22 it’s still 1.1, active development (the --experimental-sqlite flag went away in 22.13, the label didn’t), so a server on Node 22 is running an API the docs describe as “nearing minimum viability”. Where it does less: better-sqlite3 has db.transaction(fn) , which wraps a function in BEGIN , COMMIT and ROLLBACK for you, and node:sqlite has nothing like it. You write those three statements yourself in a try / catch . articles.title: Tibetan-Singing-Bowls: Strike or rub a set of virtual Tibetan singing bowls - synthesized in the browser with Web Audio, with the beating overtones of the real thing
articles.content: Play a set of virtual Tibetan singing bowls right in your browser. Strike a bowl, or hold it down to draw the tone out the way a mallet circles the rim. The sound is synthesized live, so there are no audio files to load, and it works offline. Use headphones or good speakers. Seven bowls are tuned to a scale, each with its own color. Tap or click a bowl to strike it. Switch to Sing and hold a bowl down to make it swell and sustain, then let go to let it fade. The number keys 1 to 7 play the bowls from the keyboard, and you can play several at once. Tuning : a seven-note chakra scale (C to B, one bowl per chakra) or a pentatonic scale, in the low, middle or high octave, with A at 440 Hz or 432 Hz. Sound : volume and room reverb. Spectrum : a live view of the sound, so you can watch the overtones rise and fade. Sound bath : press start and pick 5, 10, 20 or 30 minutes, and the bowls play by themselves, one strike at a time, with silence in between. A struck bowl rings at its fundamental plus overtones at about 2.7, 5.2 and 8.3 times that pitch. Those overtones are not whole-number multiples, which is why a bowl sounds like a bell and not like a string. Each partial is made of two sine oscillators a fraction of a hertz apart, so it swells and fades a few times a second: that beating is the "wah-wah" of a real bowl. Higher partials die away faster. The result goes through a synthesized room reverb and a compressor. This is a model of the sound and not a recording. The bowls are not meant as a medical treatment, and the chakra colors are a common convention, not a measurement. The pages are plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with the Web Audio API, with no dependencies and no build step. Just open index.html . It is also a small installable web app: add it to your home screen or desktop and it works offline. The bowls are drawn as SVG. The app logic is in js/bowls.js . Three color themes (dark, light and blue) are shared with my other projects. Your tuning, volume and other settings are kept in the browser's local storage. Tibetan-Singing-Bowls is open source at GitHub with MIT license. Had fun browsing the app? Buy me a coffee by becoming a sponsor . articles.content: Draw a mandala right in your browser. Whatever you draw is repeated around the center and mirrored, so a few loose strokes become a symmetric design. Save it as a PNG or as an SVG. articles.title: Supapower - A sync engine that keeps a local PGlite database in sync with Supabase, inspired by PowerSync
articles.content: Supapower is a sync engine that keeps a local PGlite database in sync with Supabase , so an application can read and write locally and stay usable while offline. It is inspired by PowerSync . Status: 0.3.0. Both directions of the sync work; the public API may still change before 1.0. Nothing new to deploy - Supabase's Data API and Realtime are the sync protocol; no sync service, no replication slot, no second bill. Real Postgres on both ends - the client is PGlite, not SQLite: the same SQL, the same types, and migrations you can lift from the server. Your RLS policies are the sync rules - downloads and writes go through PostgREST as the signed-in user, so there is no second authorization language to keep in step. Two-way sync that merges per column - offline writes queue per transaction and upload only the columns that changed, so two people editing different fields of a row both keep their edit. Three lines to adopt - a PGlite extension plus one sync() call; no codegen, no schema DSL, no client-side query language to learn. Small, permissive, batteries included - Apache-2.0 with zero runtime dependencies, plus a SharedWorker multi-tab host, React and Vue bindings, and a typed status and event API. Longer version, and how it compares with RxDB, PowerSync, Electric and Zero: supapower.dev/why-supapower · supapower.dev/comparison Everything below, except the examples section , is for working with the monorepo. For documentation on the Supapower library see the supapower package's readme , or the full documentation site at supapower.dev . Package Description supapower The main package for Supapower - a PGlite extension that integrates with Supabase and syncs data between them @supapower/worker A more stable drop-in replacement for PGlite's built-in multi-tab worker, using a SharedWorker with automatic fallback - works with plain PGlite, no Supapower required @supapower/react React hooks for Supapower: PGlite live queries plus sync status @supapower/vue Vue composables for Supapower: PGlite live queries plus sync status Example Description chat A terminal chat app, showing a two-way sync between Supabase and PGlite vue-chat A browser chat app, showing @supapower/worker 's multi-tab SharedWorker and a two-way sync between Supabase and PGlite Bun 1.4 or later, used as package manager, test runner and script runner Node.js 22 or later or a modern browser for consumers of the published packages bun install bun run check bun run check runs the same four steps as continuous integration: lint, format check, typecheck and tests. articles.title: 做了个网页电台：随机一站，听听世界上 3.5 万个电台此刻在播什么
articles.content:
上班路上喜欢听广播，但经常听到一半就到公司了；平时干活的时候也想听点新鲜的，不想翻来覆去总是歌单里那几首；偶尔听到一首好听的，还得赶紧翻出音乐 App 去识别是什么歌。

所以就做了这么个小玩意：打开网页按一下，随机掉进世界上某个城市的电台，听听那里此刻在播什么。

## 能做什么

- **路上没听完**：每个台都有分享链接，到公司在电脑上打开接着听；同一个浏览器下次打开，会停在上次听的台
- **想听点新鲜的**：按「下一站」随机换台，连续翻台时会提前缓冲后面几台，基本是秒切；可以只听高码率（≥128 / 192 / 320 kbps ），也可以在设置里只留想听的语言
- **听到好歌**：能读到曲名的台，直接显示在播什么歌；读不到的点「识别这首歌」就行；曲名旁边点 ♡ 收藏，顺手跳到网易云、QQ 音乐、Spotify 去搜
- 能读到曲名的台还可以开跟唱歌词
- 星图按流派把电台铺开，可以拖着逛；也有地球视图
- 一条线路不通会自动换下一条
- 没有账号，没有广告，收藏只存在你的浏览器里

## 技术

前端 React + three.js （星图是几万个粒子），后端 Node + SQLite ，电台目录来自社区维护的 Radio Browser ，每周自动刷新、探测哪些台能播。

## 已知问题

- 部分海外电台在国内网络下可能连不上或比较慢
- iPhone 上的秒切效果还没实测

地址： https://roamdial.com （手机、电脑浏览器直接打开，不用装 App ）

欢迎试试，坏掉的台、标错的地点、想法都可以回帖，或者发邮件到 hello@roamdial.com

articles.title: 一个人可以内向，敏感，胆小到什么程度
articles.content:
印象深刻的几件小事：
1. 小学，有个堂伯在学校当老师，同时在学校里面开了个小卖部，我去上学，我爸让我带块肉给这个堂伯，我一直放在书包里，没有给他，放学回家肉都臭了，被打了一顿。我记得是我故意不给的，当时应该是怕过去，在小卖部当着众人的面，其中有很多老师，拿出一块肉。
2. 初中，有次迟到了，班主任把我单独叫出去，记得班主任也没说什么重的话，我眼泪在眼珠打转，但是没有哭出来，好像犯了很大的错一样。
3. 高中毕业暑假，跟几个朋友回初中学校打球，当时初中的班主任老师，一直站在球场边，应该是想让我上去打招呼，但是我硬生生没上去，当作没有认出他来。其实这个班主任对我很好的，因为当时成绩在班里是数一数二的。现在回想起来很很后悔，为什么没有上去打招呼。
4. 从小学到高中，一般下课，很多同学都会去楼下活动，打球或者其他活动，我是不敢单独下去的。因为想到教学楼上这么多同学，被这么多人看到，很尬尴。

以上这种情况，是到大学后才有所改善，现在工作了，也不怕在会上发言了。我也不知道怎么突然就改变了。

现在小孩男孩子，好像也继承了我的这种性格:
1. 说一句稍微重的话，就会哭，或者生气，很敏感。
2. 去陌生地方或者公共场合，和家长说话都很小声。
3. 不敢上足球场，其他小朋友都在踢，不敢上去踢。只愿意跟我在旁边踢。
4. 在家里或者学校，吃零食，怕被人看到，会躲着吃，被我老婆称之为偷感很重。
